title: The Economic Calendar
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/0/body: The **economic calendar** shows when economic news comes out: the **time, the currency involved, the impact level** (usually shown with colors or stars) and three numbers: **actual, forecast and previous**.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/1/title: The surprise matters, not the number
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/1/body: The market has already priced in the **forecast**. What creates the move is **how far the actual number is from the forecast (the surprise)**. The bigger that gap, the bigger the reaction usually is.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/2/prompt: How does this CPI number compare with what the market expected?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/2/explan: You compare against the forecast: 3.4% is above 3.1%, so inflation is hotter than the market expected.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/3/statem: If the actual number exactly matches the forecast, the market's reaction is usually smaller than after a big surprise.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/3/explan: A number in line with expectations was already in the price. Still, details in the report or the core number can move the market.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/4/body: Not all news carries the same weight. **High-impact** news like rate decisions, CPI and NFP usually causes the most volatility. Set the calendar's **time zone** to your own clock so you don't get the news time wrong.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/4/tip: At the start of each week, mark that week's high-impact news.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/5/pairs/: How much the news may move prices
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/6/prompt: You're trading EUR/USD. News for which currencies affects this pair most directly?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/6/explan: Every pair is made of two currencies. Economic news from the eurozone and the US directly affects EUR/USD.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/7/senten: The market has already priced in the ___ number, so the main move comes from how far the ___ number is from it.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/7/explan: The forecast is what the market expects. The surprise is the gap between the actual number and that expectation.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/8/statem: The "previous" number on the economic calendar never changes.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l1/steps/8/explan: Some reports, like NFP, revise earlier periods' numbers. A big revision can matter as much as the new number.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/title: Trading the news and its risks
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/0/body: The moment big news comes out, the **spread** often gets several times wider, **slippage** is common, and price can whip **both ways**. Even your stop loss may fill at a worse price.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/1/prompt: NFP just came out. Tap the candle that most likely hit the stop losses of both buyers and sellers.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/1/explan: The upper wick is about 40 pips and the lower wick is about 40 pips too, but the candle closed almost where it opened. Price went one way, then came back, and both groups got stopped out.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/2/body: 1) **Stay out**: close your position before the news or make it smaller. 2) **Wait**: for example, wait 15 to 30 minutes, then read the new structure. 3) **Trade the release** with a very small size, which is mostly for experienced traders.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/2/tip: If big news is coming, allow for slippage when you set your stop loss.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/3/prompt: You have an open position that's 20 pips in profit, and NFP comes out in 10 minutes. What's the more careful move?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/3/option: Close all or part of it, or cut your risk before the news
Double your size before the news
Remove your stop loss so the news whipsaw can't knock you out
Raise your leverage, since volatility means profit
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/3/explan: News volatility can turn your profit into a loss in seconds. Cutting risk before the news is a management decision, not fear.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/4/statem: When big news comes out, your stop loss always fills at exactly the price you set.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/4/explan: When price jumps and liquidity is thin, a stop loss order fills at the first available price, which may be worse than the one you picked.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/5/prompt: Put the routine for a big-news day in order:
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/5/items/: Morning: check the news time on the calendar
Before the news: cut or close positions
Once it calms down: read the new structure
If there's a setup: enter with your usual size
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/5/explan: First you need to know when the news is, then cut your risk before it, watch the release from the sidelines, and only enter once the market calms down and forms a setup.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/6/prompt: Hot CPI came out and EUR/USD broke support. Now price has pulled back to just below the broken level. Using the "wait and read the structure" approach, which way is more likely?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/6/explan: After the volatility calmed down, price retested the broken level from below and couldn't close above it. Old support is now acting as resistance, and the news points down too. A continued drop is more likely, but not guaranteed, so you need a stop loss above the level.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/7/senten: During big news, the ___ widens and your order may fill with ___.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l2/steps/7/explan: Liquidity drops at news time, so the gap between buy and sell prices widens and orders fill at different prices.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/0/body: When a central bank or one of its officials is **worried about inflation** and hints at **higher interest rates** (or keeping rates high for longer), their tone is called **hawkish**. A hawkish tone is usually **good** for that currency.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/1/body: When the focus is on **supporting growth and jobs** and hinting at **rate cuts**, the tone is **dovish**, and that's usually **bad** for the currency. The market cares more about a **change in tone** from last time than the tone itself.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/2/prompt: The Fed chair says: "Inflation is still too high, and we're ready to raise rates again if needed." What's this tone?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/2/explan: Worry about inflation and readiness to hike rates is the definition of a hawkish tone. It's usually good for the dollar.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/3/statem: If the ECB says "Growth has weakened and we're considering a rate cut", this dovish tone usually puts downward pressure on EUR/USD.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/3/explan: Hinting at a rate cut makes the euro less attractive, so EUR/USD usually leans down.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/4/body: The market compares the tone with its **expectations**. If everyone expects 3 rate cuts and the central bank only talks about 2, the message reads as **hawkish**, even though it's still cutting rates.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/4/tip: After the meeting, the central bank chair's press conference sometimes matters more than the decision itself.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/5/statem: A rate cut is always bad for the currency, even if the market expected a bigger cut.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/5/explan: If the market had priced in a bigger cut, a smaller one is hawkish relative to expectations, and the currency may even strengthen.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/6/senten: A ___ tone means leaning toward higher rates, and a ___ tone means leaning toward rate cuts.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/6/explan: The hawk stands for being tough on inflation, and the dove stands for focusing on growth and lower rates.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/7/prompt: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) surprised with a hawkish tone. What does the highlighted candle on USD/JPY show?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/7/option: The yen got stronger vs. the dollar
The dollar got stronger vs. the yen
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/7/explan: A hawkish BoJ is good for the yen. USD/JPY fell, meaning each dollar buys fewer yen, so the yen got stronger.
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/8/prompt: The Fed held rates steady but said "we haven't ruled out another hike." How is this message usually read?
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/8/option: Hawkish, since the path ahead is tough
Dovish, since it didn't raise rates
lessons/fundamental-u2-l3/steps/8/explan: The market looks at the path ahead. Holding rates while hinting at a possible hike counts as a "hawkish pause".
